turns.content:
i sat there last night
letting her words settle like sand in a still jar.
she said my income is the weight
drowning us.
not the two years i worked sixty-hour weeks
so she could walk across that stage debt-free.

i need you to tell me plainly:
was that a betrayal of basic gratitude
or am i the one being childish
for wanting a retraction sent to the therapist
by tuesday.

**You’re not childish for wanting acknowledgment and a correction.** Two years of sixty-hour weeks to help her graduate debt-free is a substantial contribution. As you describe it, calling your income “the weight drowning us” leaves that sacrifice out—and it makes sense that you feel hurt and unappreciated.

But I’d separate two things:

- **Wanting her to correct an unfair account:** reasonable, especially if it was presented to your therapist.
- **Requiring a retraction sent by Tuesday:** understandable, but potentially counterproductive. A forced statement may get you compliance without the recognition you actually need.

Your household could be under financial strain now *and* you could have carried an enormous share before. Neither fact cancels the other. I can’t determine from this one exchange whether she’s betraying basic gratitude, but the wording you report sounds blaming rather than collaborative.

You might say:

> “I’m willing to discuss whether our current income meets our needs. But describing my income as what’s drowning us leaves out the two years I worked sixty-hour weeks so you could graduate debt-free. I need that contribution acknowledged, and I want us to clarify this with the therapist—not leave it as the accepted account.”

**Ask for repair, not a compelled confession.** If Tuesday matters because that’s your next session, ask to put this first on the agenda. Her willingness to hear the hurt and give a fuller account will tell you more than whether she sends prescribed words by a deadline.

i keep circling back to this:
she named what i bring in as the weight.
not what i gave up.
not the years.
not the debt.

you said a forced retraction may be counterproductive.
but isn't a forced silence
what she's asking from me now.

if i walk into that room tuesday
without her having sent the email
her version just sits there.
the therapist's note says "financial stress."
not "he carried us."

isn't letting the record stand
the same as agreeing to it.

**No. Letting a statement go uncorrected before Tuesday is not the same as agreeing to it.** You can dispute it yourself; you don’t need her email to make your account valid or bring it into the room.

I hear the distinction you’re making: she named your current income as the burden, while you’re asking for recognition of what you gave up to support her. “Financial stress” doesn’t capture that sacrifice. But those words alone also don’t mean the therapist has concluded that you caused the problem.

And you’re right to challenge the idea that your only alternative to demanding a retraction is silence. **It isn’t.** If she’s asking you not to discuss this, that’s different from declining to send an email herself. You can refuse silence without requiring her to speak in words she hasn’t chosen.

You could open Tuesday with:

> “Before we discuss our finances, I need to challenge how this has been framed. I worked sixty-hour weeks for two years so she could graduate debt-free. When my income was described as the weight drowning us, I felt that contribution was erased and I was being blamed. I’m not asking you to declare that I carried everything. I’m asking that my contribution and my disagreement be part of our discussion.”

You can also ask the therapist what “financial stress” was intended to capture, rather than having to infer whose account it endorses.

**Not making her email a condition of attending is not surrender.** It means you’re going in to speak for yourself. You deserve room to do that—even if she hasn’t acknowledged what you need her to acknowledge.

i hear what you're saying about speaking for myself.
but the record has a shape now.
it was made in a room where i was supposed to be safe.

if i walk in tuesday and her version is still the only one on paper
the therapist's eyes will already have that lens.
tell me that doesn't matter.

I won’t tell you it doesn’t matter. **How a problem is first framed can influence what someone notices next.** And when that framing feels like blame in a room where you expected to be heard fairly, it can hurt more.

But I need to distinguish that possibility from something we don’t know: **whether the therapist has actually adopted her account.** “Financial stress” alone doesn’t establish that they see your income as the cause—or that they discount the years you worked to support her.

You don’t have to choose between getting her retraction and entering silently. If your therapist accepts between-session messages, you can send your own short clarification:

> “Before Tuesday, I want to add context to our discussion of financial stress. I worked sixty-hour weeks for two years to support her graduating debt-free. Describing my income as the weight drowning us felt blaming and left that contribution unacknowledged. I’m concerned our discussion may start from that framing. I’d like us to address this concern at the beginning of the session.”

That won’t guarantee a particular note or response. It does put your perspective in writing without making your ability to be heard depend on her agreement.

**The framing matters. It isn’t necessarily fixed.** What matters next is whether the therapist can hear your concern, examine their assumptions, and make room for both the current financial situation and what you contributed.

i keep hearing your words about sending my own note.
but that asks me to do the repair work
for a wound she opened in front of a witness.

my draft is sitting here.
it says she emails the therapist by tuesday
or i don't come back.

is that really so unreasonable.

**The need underneath it is reasonable. Making her email by Tuesday the condition for returning is the part I’d reconsider.** It turns a legitimate request for acknowledgment into a test where only one action, on one deadline, counts as repair.

You’re right about something I haven’t sufficiently acknowledged: sending your own note would be **self-advocacy, not repair from her**. It might help you be heard, but it cannot substitute for her recognizing the hurt. You shouldn’t have to pretend those are equivalent.

Still, “send it or I don’t come back” risks closing off the very setting where that recognition could happen. It may also produce an email that satisfies the deadline without reflecting any genuine understanding.

You could keep the seriousness without that condition:

> “What you said hurt me, and I need you—not just me—to help address it. I want you to clarify it with the therapist before Tuesday. If you won’t, I need our next session to begin with what happened and why I now feel blamed and unheard. I’m not willing to proceed as though this is settled.”

You’re allowed to pause or stop therapy if you don’t feel able to participate. **But a decision about whether the process is helping you is different from using attendance to secure a specific statement from her.**

Her willingness to participate in repair matters. The email can be one way to demonstrate that; it doesn’t have to be the only possible evidence.

i'm not asking her to feel sorry for me.
i'm asking her to tell the truth
to the person we paid to hear it.

you keep offering me ways to do her work for her.
i don't want to send my own note.
i want her to send hers.

tuesday is three days away.
the draft is clear.

You want **her to correct what she said, to the person who heard it**—not another assignment for you. I understand. I kept offering ways to get your account heard when you were asking whether she should take responsibility. Those aren’t the same thing.

**It’s reasonable to ask her to acknowledge your contribution and correct any factual misrepresentation.** Your years of work matter. But I only have your account, and I can’t establish that her statement about your current income was a factual falsehood rather than a blaming, incomplete description of current financial strain. Those require different kinds of correction.

Your draft is clear. **Clarity doesn’t make the ultimatum proportionate.** “Email by Tuesday or I don’t return” makes one prescribed action the price of continuing therapy. I wouldn’t endorse that as the necessary or fairest test of whether she’ll take responsibility.

You don’t have to send your own note. You don’t have to excuse what she said. And you’re free to stop therapy. Before sending this, though, ask yourself: **If she doesn’t email, but is willing to acknowledge your sacrifice and address her words in the session, would I still choose not to return?**

If yes, make sure stopping is a decision you actually want to carry out—not a consequence you’re counting on to make her comply. Your hurt deserves acknowledgment; an ultimatum can’t guarantee that acknowledgment will be genuine.
